proof:
# Section-centroid constraints at stochastic capacity maxima

This is a new necessary-condition mechanism for the higher-dimensional
stochastic capacity question. It retains actual simplex sections. It does
not prove containment in D_d beyond the already proved zero-row boundary.

Use m=d+1, d>=1, the capacity phi_d and D_d defined in
`candidate 8095e181b6be7bf1`.
Consider a maximum over column-stochastic X of

    H(X)=sum_i c_i phi_d(X_i),       c_i>0.                    (1)

The statements involving a fully positive row's gradient explicitly assume
that its minimizing threshold is a unique proper regular cut and that its
capacity is differentiable there. This condition must not silently be
assumed at repeated maximum knots or at a full cut.
Here a proper regular cut means an interior threshold where F_x(t) is
C^1 jointly in the row x and threshold t, with the coarea derivative
identities used below. A sufficient condition is that x is nonconstant
and t differs from every entry of x.

## 1. The exact one-sided derivative at a zero

For positive b_1,...,b_d put g=GM(b), y=min b_j. Then

    d/depsilon phi_d(epsilon,b_1,...,b_d) at 0+
       =g[1/y-(sum_j 1/b_j)/d].                          (2)

The formula remains valid with repeated positive b_j. Here is a proof
without differentiating at a repeated knot. For epsilon<y, at thresholds
epsilon<t<=y the cap ratio is exactly

    [product_j(b_j-epsilon)]^(1/d) t/(t-epsilon),

and is decreasing in t. Any minimizing threshold t_epsilon is therefore
at least y; it can be chosen at most max b_j. For the row with epsilon=0,
the ratio is constant g up to y and strictly larger for t>y. The strictness
follows directly from the scaled orthant description: as soon as t>y,
the extra constraint sum u<=1 removes a set of positive volume from the
orthant simplex b dot u<=t. Thus compactness and the upper bound obtained
by choosing t=y give t_epsilon->y.

For every threshold, the full orthant simplex is an upper bound on the
captured simplex volume. Consequently the minimizing value is at least

    [product_j(b_j-epsilon)]^(1/d)
                          t_epsilon/(t_epsilon-epsilon).

It is at most the same expression with t_epsilon replaced by y. Expanding
these two bounds to first order proves (2). If all b_j=y, the capacity is
exactly y for every epsilon<y, and the same formula gives zero. This also
handles d=1.

## 2. A positive row excludes partially supported zero-capacity rows

If a maximizer of (1) has a fully positive row, then every other nonzero
row either is fully positive or has exactly one zero. In particular a
nonzero row with between two and d zeros is impossible.

Indeed leave one of that row's zeros unchanged and add epsilon to each
of its other zero entries, funding these changes from the fully positive
row in the same columns. If there were r zeros, the formerly zero capacity
becomes C epsilon^((r-1)/d) with C>0, by the exact zero-row geometric-mean
formula. Since 2<=r<=d, its exponent is strictly less than one. The loss
in the funding row is only O(epsilon). To see the latter without assuming
differentiability, if the row's minimum entry is a>0 then a perturbation
of coordinate sup norm epsilon lies coordinatewise between
(1-epsilon/a)x and (1+epsilon/a)x. Capacity is monotone and homogeneous,
so this gives the claimed Lipschitz bound. The positive gain dominates,
contradicting maximality. An identically zero row is a separate status;
the same argument does not exclude it.

## 3. A full regular row records an actual section centroid

Let x be positive and have a unique proper regular minimizing threshold t.
Write F=F_x(t), and let b_j be the mean barycentric coordinate Xi_j on the
actual section {x dot Xi=t}, with its ordinary coarea measure normalized
to a probability measure. Then

    partial_j phi_d(x)=F^(-1/d) b_j.                      (3)

The coarea derivative is
partial_j F_x(t)=-F'_x(t)b_j. At an interior minimizing threshold,
t F'_x(t)=dF_x(t). For a fixed minimizing threshold, the corresponding ratio is a smooth
upper support for phi_d, with equality at x. Since phi_d is assumed
differentiable here, applying this inequality in opposite coordinate
directions makes their gradients equal. The coarea identity and the
vanishing threshold derivative therefore give (3), with no derivative of
a selected minimizer required. Every b_j is positive, their
sum is one, and x dot b=t. The positivity follows because this proper
section meets the relative interior of the simplex.

At a maximum (1), two fully positive regular rows have identical weighted
gradients: arbitrary column-preserving transfers between them are feasible
in both signs. Thus their normalized section-centroid vectors are the
same. This is a geometric compatibility condition on the actual sections,
not merely an assertion about their marginal volumes.

## 4. Column multipliers forced by the zero rows

Suppose a maximizer has at least one full regular row. Its weighted
gradient supplies strictly positive column multipliers lambda_j. A transfer
between that row and any positive entry of another row gives equality of
the corresponding derivatives.

For a row i with unique zero column h, put g_i=phi_d(X_i)>0 and
mu_i=c_i g_i/d. Its positive entries satisfy

    X_ij=mu_i/lambda_j       (j!=h),
    c_i=d GM((lambda_j)_{j!=h}).                         (4)

Funding an increase at the missing entry from the full row and using (2)
now gives the exact restriction

    d max_{j!=h}lambda_j <= sum_j lambda_j.               (5)

Indeed the weighted one-sided derivative at that missing entry equals
 d max_{j!=h}lambda_j-sum_{j!=h}lambda_j, and must be at most lambda_h.
If two such rows have different missing columns, (5) implies

    lambda_j <= (sum lambda)/d for every j.              (6)

For an identically zero row i, instead add epsilon times an arbitrary
nonnegative row with a chosen zero column h, again funded from the full
row. The first-order inequality and weighted AM-GM give

    c_i<=d GM((lambda_j)_{j!=h}) for EVERY h.              (7)

These distinctions between a zero entry, a zero-capacity nonzero row,
and an identically zero row are necessary.

## 5. Exact additional equations with just one full row

Suppose exactly one row r is full and regular. Rows sharing a missing
column in (4) have the same c_i and proportional positive entries. They
can be merged without changing (1), since geometric mean is homogeneous
on proportional rows. The other rows in each group become identically
zero. Permute columns so that each remaining nonzero zero-row has its
zero on its diagonal; the unmatched columns can be assigned arbitrarily
to the remaining row labels, including r.

Let x be the full row and let mu_j=0 for the full-row label and for every
identically zero row; retain the positive mu_j in (4) for the other rows.
Set mu=sum_j mu_j and S=sum_j lambda_j. Column stochasticity becomes

    lambda_j(1-x_j)=mu-mu_j.                             (8)

By homogeneity and the column sums, H(X)=S. Equation (3) identifies the
full row's section centroid as b_j=lambda_j/S, and its minimizing
threshold as t=x dot b. Summing (8) and using
c_r phi_d(x)=S t gives

    mu=S(1-t)/d.

Consequently the ACTUAL full-row section satisfies

    (1-x_j)b_j/(1-t) <= 1/d for every j,                 (9)

with equality at every label having mu_j=0, in particular at j=r.
Here 0<t<1 because the full row is a proper regular cut and every entry
is in (0,1]; equation (8) also forces t<1 whenever a nonzero zero-row is
present. A putative one-full-row maximum with no other nonzero row has
x=(1,...,1), whose cut is not regular and is explicitly outside this
section's hypothesis.

The left side in (9) is a pushforward centroid coordinate: apply
the diagonal affine map Xi_j -> (1-x_j)Xi_j/(1-t) to the full-row section
with its normalized coarea measure. The image lies in the probability
simplex and this pushforward probability has centroid given by (9).
Coordinates with x_j=1 may collapse; therefore no invertibility of this
map is asserted. When all x_j<1 the map is invertible on the section and
ordinary uniform section measure transforms by one constant Jacobian.

Equations (4)--(9) retain actual incidence and section-centroid data that
are discarded by scalar density or probability-only capacity bounds.
They do not yet imply the missing support inequality for the full row.
In particular the proposed scalar Schur-product replacement was disproved
by the separate exact tetrahedral row (1/16,1/4,1,1), and is not used here.
